{{Short description|Operator theorem}}
In [[operator theory]], the '''commutant lifting theorem''', due to [[Béla Szőkefalvi-Nagy|Sz.-Nagy]] and [[Ciprian Foias|Foias]], is a powerful theorem used to prove several interpolation results.

==Statement==
The commutant lifting theorem states that if <math>T</math> is a [[contraction (operator theory)|contraction]] on a [[Hilbert space]] <math>H</math>, <math>U</math> is its minimal unitary [[Dilation (operator theory)|dilation]] acting on some Hilbert space <math>K</math> (which can be shown to exist by [[Sz.-Nagy's dilation theorem]]), and <math>R</math> is an operator on <math>H</math> commuting with <math>T</math>, then there is an operator <math>S</math> on <math>K</math> commuting with <math>U</math> such that
:<math>R T^n = P_H S U^n \vert_H \; \forall n \geq 0,</math>

and

:<math>\Vert S \Vert = \Vert R \Vert.</math>

Here, <math>P_H</math> is the [[Projection (mathematics)|projection]] from <math>K</math> onto <math>H</math>. In other words, an operator from the [[commutant]] of ''T'' can be "lifted" to an operator in the commutant of the unitary dilation of ''T''.

==Applications==
The commutant lifting theorem can be used to prove the left [[Nevanlinna-Pick interpolation]] theorem, the [[Sarason interpolation theorem]], and the two-sided Nudelman theorem, among others.

===The Nevanlinna-Pick interpolation theorem===

A classical application of the commutant lifting theorem is in solving the [[Nevanlinna-Pick interpolation]] problem. The points for which the interpolation problem has a solution can be characterized precisely in terms of the [[Definite matrix|positive semi-definiteness]] of a certain [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] constructed from the points.

{{math theorem|name=Theorem (Nevanlinna-Pick interpolation)|''Let <math>z_1,\dots,z_n\in\mathbb D</math> and <math>w_1,\dots,w_n\in\mathbb D</math>''. The following are equivalent:
# ''There exists a holomorphic function <math>\varphi:\mathbb D\to\mathbb D</math> with <math>\varphi(z_j)=w_j</math> for <math>j=1,\dots,n</math>''.
# ''The Pick matrix <math>\left(\frac{1-w_i\overline w_j}{1-z_i\overline z_j}\right)_{i,j=1}^n</math> is positive semi-definite''.}}

The main idea behind the proof is to consider the [[Hardy space]] <math>H^2(\mathbb D)</math> of the disc <math>\mathbb D</math> and use that this is a [[reproducing kernel Hilbert space]] with multipliers the space <math>H^\infty(\mathbb D)</math> of bounded holomorphic functions on <math>\mathbb D</math>. The [[reproducing kernel]] of <math>H^2(\mathbb D)</math> is the function
:<math>k(z,w)=\frac{1}{1-z\overline w}</math>
commonly referred to as the [[Szegő kernel]]. The tricky part of the proof is showing that the condition of positive semi-definiteness implies the existence of said interpolating function. Following [[Jim Agler|J. Agler]] and [[John McCarthy (mathematician)|J. McCarthy]] the idea of the proof is as follows.<ref>{{cite book|author=J. Agler and J. E. McCarthy|title=Pick interpolation and Hilbert function spaces| series=Graduate Studies in Mathematics|volume=44|publisher=American Mathematical Society, Providence, RI|date=2002|pages=xx+308|isbn=0-8218-2898-3|doi=10.1090/gsm/044}}</ref> Suppose that the Pick matrix is positive semi-definite. Consider, for <math>\varphi\in H^\infty(\mathbb D)</math>, the [[Linear operator|operator]] <math>M_\varphi</math> on <math>H^2(\mathbb D)</math> given by multiplication by <math>\varphi</math>, meaning that
:<math>M_\varphi f(z)=\varphi(z)f(z)</math>
for <math>f\in H^2(\mathbb D)</math>. This is a [[bounded operator]] on <math>H^2(\mathbb D)</math>, and one can show that its [[Hermitian adjoint|adjoint]] <math>M_\varphi^*</math> satisfies
:<math>M_\varphi^*k(\,\cdot\,,z)=\overline{\varphi(z)}k(\,\cdot\,,z)</math>
An important special case of this is when <math>\varphi(z)=z</math>, in which case we write <math>M_z</math> for its multiplication operator. Consider next the finite-dimensional [[Linear subspace|subspace]]
:<math>S=\operatorname{span}\{k(\,\cdot\,,z_1),\dots,k(\,\cdot\,,z_n)\}</math>
of <math>H^2(\mathbb D)</math>. Define an operator <math>T</math> on <math>S</math> by letting
:<math>Tk(\,\cdot\,,z_j)=\overline w_jk(\,\cdot\,,z_j)</math>
The idea is now to extend the operator <math>T</math> to the adjoint <math>M_\varphi^*</math> of a multiplication operator on the entirety of <math>H^2(\mathbb D)</math> for some <math>\varphi</math>, where <math>\varphi</math> will then be the solution to the interpolation problem. This is where the commutant lifting theorem comes into play. In particular, one can verify that <math>S</math> is an [[invariant subspace]] of <math>M_z^*</math>, that <math>T</math> commutes with the restriction of <math>M_z^*</math> to <math>S</math>, and that <math>M_z^*</math> is co-isometric (meanining that its adjoint is [[Isometry#Linear isometry|isometric]]). Applying the commutant lifting theorem we can then find an operator <math>\tilde T</math> on <math>H^2(\mathbb D)</math> which agrees with <math>T</math> on <math>S</math>, which has the same [[Operator norm|norm]] as <math>T</math>, and which commutes with <math>M_z^*</math>. Then in particular <math>\tilde T</math> commutes with <math>M_p</math> for any [[polynomial]] <math>p</math>. By setting <math>\varphi=\tilde T\mathbf 1</math>, where <math>\mathbf 1</math> is the constant function equal to <math>1</math>, and using that the polynomials are [[Dense set|dense]] in <math>H^2(\mathbb D)</math>, one can then show that <math>\tilde T^*=M_\varphi</math>, so that <math>\tilde T=M_\varphi^*</math>. This function must then interpolate the points, as
:<math>\overline{\varphi(z_j)}k(\,\cdot\,,z_j)=M_\varphi^*k(\,\cdot\,,z_j)=\tilde Tk(\,\cdot\,,z_j)=Tk(\,\cdot\,,z_j)=\overline w_j k(\,\cdot\,,z_j),</math>
from which we get <math>\varphi(z_j)=w_j</math>. That <math>\varphi(\mathbb D)\subseteq\mathbb D</math> is then a consequence of computing
:<math>\sup_{z\in\mathbb D}|\varphi(z)|=\lVert M_\varphi\rVert=\lVert\tilde T\rVert=\lVert T\rVert,</math>
showing that <math>\lVert T\rVert\leq1</math> by showing that <math>I-T^*T</math> is [[Positive operator|positive]] (which is where the positive semi-definiteness of the Pick matrix comes in), and then finally appealing to the [[Open mapping theorem (complex analysis)|open mapping theorem]]. As such <math>\varphi</math> is the desired interpolating function.
